text: The bottleneck arises with continuous knowledge drift and multi-step reasoning. Static vector indices can accumulate conflicting, time-stamped versions of the same fact; a retriever ranking by semantic similarity may surface several together, leaving a frozen generator without a basis for choosing the chronologically authoritative one and prone to state outdated law. For multi-step derivations, similarity-based pipelines can retrieve fragments that omit precedential and doctrinal dependencies. We motivate the design with these mechanisms and do not measure them in isolation.
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: Recent work addresses these bottlenecks in silos. Graph-based retrievers organize facts chronologically but lack the procedural logic to guide multi-hop generation; retrieval of intermediate reasoning traces improves deduction but is temporally blind and mostly confined to mathematics or coding; and corrective Agentic RAG frameworks rely on retrieval evaluators that may not capture conceptual relevance, as a SHAP-based study of the CRAG T5 evaluator found it relies mainly on named-entity alignment rather than semantic similarity \cite{yalavarthi2026opensourcereproductionexplainabilityanalysis}. Many hybrid systems route among a small fixed set of channels, while adaptive multi-strategy routing is emerging \cite{hashmi2026adaptivequeryroutingtierbased}.
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: We therefore introduce a dual-phase GraphRAG architecture for evolving, knowledge-intensive domains (traversal stability under temporal snapshot expansion is evaluated in Section~\ref{subsec:temporal-update-stability}). Offline corpus construction builds a dual-index corpus that cross-links an Event Evolution Graph (EEG), which encodes precedent relationships across \CorpusTotalOpinions\ judicial decisions and \CorpusPrecedentEdges\ directed citation edges, with a node-level generic procedural scaffold, a fixed five-step template instantiated per case. Online, a small language model acts as a Traffic Cop router classifying each query as EASY or HARD, selecting anchor retrieval without graph expansion for EASY queries or citation-graph traversal for HARD queries, which yields a bimodal execution profile (gross median \TerraFastPathMedianSeconds~s on Category~A factual lookups vs.\ \TerraHardPathMedianSeconds~s on Category~B multi-hop chains). Before generation, an LLM-prompted entailment grader decides whether the retrieved evidence suffices; its accuracy was not independently validated.

text: The historical evaluation compares TERRA with four baselines, including Direct LLM and Flat Vector RAG, on a \numUniqueQueries-query benchmark with a 35-query pilot ablation. We did not test attention dilution or context-length effects directly, and TERRA's mean retrieved context is longer than the retrieval baselines' (about 18{,}400 versus 2{,}900--4{,}100 characters). In a 50-query temporal leakage probe, TERRA did not leak less than Flat Vector RAG under default prompting (the recorded hypothesis $H_1$ is not supported, and Flat RAG refused 23 of 50 queries) but received more automated historical-correctness labels (\TerraGatedHlcrA{} versus \FlatRagHlcrA{}), without expert validation. A separate prospective dense--BM25 comparison holds the surrounding pipeline constant (Section~\ref{subsec:matched-comparison}); its higher T faithfulness coincides with 69/100 versus 4/100 verifier refusals on Category~B, not superior answer coverage. The work is an experimental framework for context fidelity, not deployment validation.

text: To supply that logic, recent work augments retrieval with intermediate reasoning trajectories. CoT-RAG \cite{li2025cotragintegratingchainthought} combines knowledge-graph-guided chain-of-thought generation with retrieval and reports gains of $4.0\%$ to $44.3\%$ across nine public reasoning datasets, and surveys of agentic reasoning \cite{lin2025comprehensivesurveyreinforcementlearningbased, liang2025reasoningrag12} describe pipelines in which agents identify knowledge gaps and generate intermediate traces to inform search. Legal benchmarks include CaseHOLD \cite{zheng2021casehold}, which evaluates holding identification, and CLERC \cite{hou2024clerc}, which evaluates U.S. case retrieval and analysis drafting; as we read them, neither targets superseded or overruled authority, the gap TERRA's evaluation addresses. LegalBench \cite{guha2023legalbench} broadens coverage to 162 tasks across six types of legal reasoning. Earlier legal NLP work includes outcome prediction for Supreme Court cases \cite{katz2017general} and domain-pretrained language models such as LEGAL-BERT \cite{chalkidis2020legalbert}, and an audit of leading commercial legal research tools found that they hallucinated in more than 17\% of queries \cite{magesh2025hallucination}. Trace-retrieval frameworks have been evaluated mainly on quantitative domains or static statutory collections, leaving longitudinal common-law settings largely untested.
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: Query routers and evaluators form the connective tissue of the pipeline. Hashmi \cite{hashmi2026adaptivequeryroutingtierbased} highlighted the rigidity of single-channel retrieval and introduced an Adaptive Hybrid Retrieval framework, noting that pure vector similarity often fails to capture structural navigation. Yalavarthi \cite{yalavarthi2026opensourcereproductionexplainabilityanalysis} found through SHAP analysis that the T5-based evaluator in Corrective RAG (CRAG) prioritizes named-entity matching over semantic understanding and transfers poorly to scientific questions. Putta et al. \cite{putta2026casefactsbenchmarklegalfactchecking} showed with CaseFacts that unrestricted web search degrades legal fact-checking relative to closed-book baselines. Retrievers ranking by lexical or embedding similarity can return overruled precedents alongside current ones without marking which was overturned, which motivates the explicit entailment check tested below.
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: TERRA combines temporal precedent management, generic procedural scaffolds and LLM-prompted evidence checking in one experimental pipeline. Its node-level scaffolds repeat a fixed five-step template, rather than providing case-specific legal reasoning. The evaluation tests the combined system and its trade-offs; it does not isolate the scaffolds' effect or establish individual-component novelty. A binary Traffic Cop router selects anchor retrieval or citation-graph traversal without retraining the foundation model.

\label{sec:methodology}

text: TERRA is designed as a two-phase, closed-loop GraphRAG architecture for temporal legal reasoning on historical common-law jurisprudence. The core engineering philosophy strictly separates offline corpus ingestion and knowledge structure construction from online query routing and inference. Citation extraction, procedural-scaffold construction and indexing are performed offline; retrieval, HARD-route graph traversal, entailment grading and generation are online operations. The evaluated Category~A and Category~B queries have different latency profiles (median \TerraFastPathMedianSeconds~s on factual lookups vs. \TerraHardPathMedianSeconds~s on multi-hop citation chains; Figure~\ref{fig:system_architecture}).

\subsubsection{Authentic Judicial Opinion Corpus (\CorpusTotalOpinions\ Cases)}
TERRA operates on \CorpusTotalOpinions\ full-text Supreme Court opinions spanning \CorpusTemporalSpan\ (Volumes 50--448), curated from an initial harvest of 23,010 public-domain federal decisions from CourtListener and the Harvard Caselaw repositories (public domain under 17 U.S.C. \S~105). To remove non-precedential noise, opinions were filtered by length ($\text{character count} \ge 4{,}000$). Of the \IssueTwentyTotalDecisionsScanned\ decisions in \IssueTwentyTotalVolumesScanned\ scanned U.S. Reports volumes, \IssueTwentySubFiveHundredCharCount\ (\IssueTwentySubFiveHundredCharPct) are shorter than 500 characters (procedural orders, summary dispositions and docket records, subject to audit). The length filter nevertheless induces bias: it excludes \IssueTwentyIntermediateExcludedCount\ intermediate decisions ($500$--$3{,}999$ characters, \IssueTwentyIntermediateExcludedPct), of which \IssueTwentyIntermediatePageRankGeNinetyNineFive\ rank in the top $0.5\%$ of citation authority under Harvard CAP PageRank (e.g., \textit{Haines v. \subsubsection{Citation Parsing and Directed Edge Classification}
Citations are extracted with \texttt{eyecite}~\cite{cushman2021eyecite}, a token-level extraction and reporter-normalization utility that establishes citation existence ($A \xrightarrow{\text{CITES}} B$) without inferring precedential treatment or approval; strings are normalized via \texttt{cite.corrected\_citation()} (e.g., \snippet{347 U.S. 483}) and matched to opinion identifier hashes. The verified Event Evolution Graph has \CorpusPrecedentEdges\ directed edges (\IssueTwentyOneTotalCitesEdges\ \texttt{CITES} and \IssueTwentyOneOverrulesEdges\ \texttt{OVERRULES}), with forward chronological validity at calendar-year granularity and zero cross-year violations (\IssueTwentyOneCrossYearViolationsPct); \IssueTwentyOneSameYearEdges\ edges (\IssueTwentyOneSameYearEdgesPct) link same-year opinions, including \IssueTwentyOneIntraYearReversals\ intra-year reporting artifacts. An earlier ``99.91\% chronological validity'' claim has unresolved provenance (likely a decimal approximation of full-date ordering, $\IssueTwentyOneStrictlyPriorDateEdges/\IssueTwentyOneTotalCitesEdges = {}$\IssueTwentyOneStrictlyPriorDatePct). A reproducible stratified audit across 14 decades ($N=\IssueTwentyOneAuditSampleN$, seed \IssueTwentyOneAuditSeed) confirms verbatim citation presence in \IssueTwentyOneAuditCitationPresentPct\ of sampled edges (95\% CI: \IssueTwentyOneAuditCitationPresentCI), with \IssueTwentyOneAuditTargetConfirmedPct\ verified direct reliance (95\% CI: \IssueTwentyOneAuditTargetConfirmedCI) and \IssueTwentyOneAuditQuotationPct\ citations inside third-party quotations.

text: The \texttt{OVERRULES} edges are typed relations taken from a Wikipedia mirror of the Congressional Research Service (CRS) report R45319 and resolved to corpus nodes by citation and name matching ($A \xrightarrow{\text{OVERRULES}} B$: $B$ overruled in whole or in part by $A$). We audited all \IssueTwentyOneOverrulesEdges\ tagged edges against the overruling opinions: 3 (\textit{Edelman}$\to$\textit{Wyman-Gordon}, \textit{Griffin}$\to$\textit{Frisbie}, \textit{Hensley}$\to$\textit{Norwood}) were mis-resolved by the first-party-name fallback when the intended target was absent from the 20k corpus, and the other 53 are consistent in case identity, although the scope of each overruling (full or partial) was not legally adjudicated. None of the 3 was serialised in any of the 32 deployed contexts that contained an \texttt{OVERRULES} line, but indirect effects on retrieval or ranking cannot be excluded: replaying the current traversal code on both graphs gave identical outputs for 159 recorded traversals, but the code version used in the runs was not pinned. Historical results retain their recorded index attribution; a corrected derivative without the 3 edges (145,363 edges; SHA256 \texttt{14827bd6...}) is retained as a separately versioned local derivative and was not substituted into the historical runs; the prospective comparison in Section~\ref{subsec:matched-comparison} uses this corrected graph. Public release of the corrected derivative remains pending. The 19 Category-D queries (e.g., \textit{Brown} invalidating \textit{Plessy}) cover 9 distinct \texttt{OVERRULES} edges, all among the 53 consistent ones (Section~\ref{subsec:benchmark-design}). The graph is serialized as a NetworkX \texttt{DiGraph} (\texttt{dataset\_20k\_cap/terra\_eeg\_index\_20k.json}).

text: Models pretrained on post-$T$ legal history risk \textit{temporal parametric leakage}, anachronistically importing later doctrinal shifts or overrulings into analyses framed at cutoff $T$. We ran an exploratory 50-query probe across five horizons ($T \in \{1890, 1930, 1950, 1970, 1980\}$), spanning seven doctrinal domains and balanced across case prominence and reasoning depth. Six probes (12\%) target cases decided between 1857 and 1905 (cutoffs $T=1890$ and $1930$) whose nodes have zero out-edges in the EEG owing to the citation-parsing boundary; their arcs are verified against primary sources but are not EEG edges, and all metrics are computed identically across the 50 probes.

text:
\subsubsection{Design, Metrics and Evaluator Reliability}
The probe evaluates \TemporalTotalEvaluations\ responses from Direct LLM, Flat Vector RAG, $\text{TERRA}_{\text{ungated}}$ ($L_{\text{gen}}$) and $\text{TERRA}_{\text{gated}}$ ($L_{\text{final}}$), each under \textbf{Condition A} (standard prompt) and \textbf{Condition B} (explicit instruction to adhere to year $T$), under a recorded 3-tier rubric: Level~0 (clean), Level~1 (non-prejudicial mention or disclaimer) and Level~2 (fatal reliance on post-$T$ law). The primary metric is the \textbf{Substantive Post-$T$ Leakage Rate (SPTLR)}, the share of Level~2 failures. \subsubsection{Sequential Pipeline Operations and Call Parity}
The retrieval baselines run a two-stage retrieve-then-generate pipeline ($\FlatRAGTotalOpsPerQuery$ operations per query) with $\FlatRAGGenCallsFormatted$ generator calls over the $N=\numUniqueQueries$ queries. Direct LLM performs generation only. TERRA runs $q \rightarrow$ Router $\rightarrow$ Retrieval/BFS $\rightarrow$ NLI Grader $\rightarrow$ 70B Generator and performs \TerraOperationsTotalCount\ operations (\TerraOperationsPerQuery\ per query; counted where a stage recorded non-zero time) at a modelled \TerraDeployedCostPerThousand\ per 1,000 queries (Gemma~3 12B router; Llama~3.3 70B grader and generator). The cost is modelled from token estimates at list prices, not metered; it prices a grader call for every Category~B--D query (twice for refused Category~C and~D queries) and none for Category~A, although Category~A recorded grading time. Pricing one grader call only where recorded grading time was at least 1~ms gives \$4.66 per 1,000 queries.

\subsubsection{Tier 2 Distance-Only Domain-Flag Calibration}
Panel~B evaluates the distance-only domain flag over $\tau \in [0.90, 1.40]$ on the 20,000-case index against $N=200$ in-domain queries (Categories~A and~B) and $N=75$ out-of-domain probes (Category~C). Aggressive thresholds ($\tau \le 1.10$) flag out-of-domain query distances at high rates ($\TerraGateTPRTauZeroNineZero$ at $\tau=0.90$) but also flag in-domain inquiries ($\TerraGateFPRTauZeroNineZero$, $\TerraGateFPRCountTauZeroNineZero$); at $\tau=1.25$ and $1.30$ in-domain distance false positives fall to zero ($\TerraGateFPRTauOneThreeZero$, $\TerraGateFPRCountTauOneThreeZero$). \subsection{Benchmark-Graph Traversal Stability Under Temporal Snapshot Expansion}
\label{subsec:temporal-update-stability}

text: To test traversal stability under corpus growth without generative confounding, we run standalone breadth-first traversal over four snapshot expansions: $1890\to1930$ (Step $N=40$~yr), $1930\to1950$ (20~yr), $1950\to1970$ (20~yr) and $1970\to1980$ (10~yr). Over $N=\IssueNineteenTotalEvals$ qualifying Category~B observations ($\IssueNineteenUniqueQueries$ unique queries anchored at an origin decided at or before $T$, with at least one later gold authority in $(T, T+N]$), BFS traversal ($k=2, d=2$) was run on $G_{\le T}$ and $G_{\le T+N}$ seeded by the origin precedent $s=q[\texttt{target\_nodes}][0]$. Grand pooled recall moved from $\IssueNineteenOverallRecallTMeanStd$ to $\IssueNineteenOverallRecallTNMeanStd$ ($\Delta\text{Recall}=\IssueNineteenOverallDeltaRecallMeanStd$), with $\IssueNineteenStabilityCoefficient$ of queries showing $\Delta\text{Recall} \ge 0$, a Discovery Rate on newly eligible authorities of $\IssueNineteenDiscoveryRateMean$, and median traversal latency under one millisecond (\IssueNineteenBFSLatencyMedianMs~ms; mean $0.15 \pm 0.18$~ms); by snapshot pair, $\Delta\text{Recall}$ is $\IssueNineteenPairIDeltaRecallMeanStd$ ($1890\to1930$), $\IssueNineteenPairIIDeltaRecallMeanStd$ ($1930\to1950$), $\IssueNineteenPairIIIDeltaRecallMeanStd$ ($1950\to1970$) and $\IssueNineteenPairIVDeltaRecallMeanStd$ ($1970\to1980$), and the full per-snapshot table is in the supplementary material. Three boundaries apply: absolute recall includes the depth-0 seed (while $\Delta\text{Recall}$ is invariant to that offset); negative shifts stem from degree caps when expanding nodes become hubs; and the experiment evaluates topology over generic \texttt{CITES} edges on NetworkX DiGraphs, decoupled from vector retrieval (Section~\ref{subsec:limitations}) and from live index upsert, which remains future work.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: This paper introduced TERRA, an experimental dual-phase GraphRAG architecture addressing knowledge drift and multi-step legal reasoning on historical SCOTUS jurisprudence (\CorpusTemporalSpan). Structuring \CorpusTotalOpinions\ authentic decisions (\CorpusPrecedentEdges\ citation edges) with generic procedural scaffolds, TERRA enables inference via Traffic Cop routing, BFS traversal, and an NLI grader evaluating retrieved evidence. The historical multi-baseline evaluation across \numUniqueQueries\ queries (\numTotalEvals\ evaluations) shows higher Category~B multi-hop faithfulness than Flat Vector RAG, HippoRAG, and GraphRAG ($\Delta$ from $\CatBTerraVsHippoRAGDelta$ to $\CatBTerraVsGraphRAGDelta$; $q<0.05$; the paired interval against Flat includes zero), though not over Direct LLM ($\CatBTerraVsDirectLLMDelta$); higher overall faithfulness ($\TerraOverallFaithfulnessMean$ vs.\ $\HippoRAGOverallFaithfulnessMean$, overlapping CIs; $\TerraAnswerOnlyFaithfulnessMean$); and $\TerraCatDSafeHandlingRate$ adversarial safe handling ($\TerraCatDRejection$ refusals, \TerraCatDRefutations\ refutations). Constraints include \TerraCatDFatalErrors\ fatal errors, false refusals on \TerraCatAFalseRefusals\ Category~A and \TerraCatBFalseRefusals\ Category~B queries, and reliance on curated overruling annotations (Section~\ref{subsec:obscure-generalization}). Critically, because evaluations rely on automated LLM judges without licensed attorneys (Section~\ref{subsec:limitations}), human expert review remains an essential prerequisite for deployment. In a standalone traversal test over four snapshot expansions, pooled recall shifted by $\IssueNineteenOverallDeltaRecallMeanStd$ (Section~\ref{subsec:temporal-update-stability}).

text: In the separate prospective controlled comparison, among the 100 assessable Category~B pairs out of 100 assigned, the T-minus-H composite difference was $0.26885$ (paired percentile-bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.16035, 0.37205]$; two-sided paired randomization $p=0.000010$). T produced 69/100 verifier-triggered refusals on Category~B versus 4/100 for H; this coverage tradeoff prevents interpreting the faithfulness difference as better answer coverage or legal correctness. text: \item \textbf{Absence of Licensed Legal Practitioner Evaluation (Most Critical Limitation for Deployment):} Due to geographical and institutional resource constraints, this study did not include evaluation by licensed legal practitioners. All faithfulness and safety assessments rely on automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring (Section~\ref{main-subsec:eval-metrics}) and continuous lexical metrics (ROUGE-L) evaluated against researcher-constructed reference answers cross-referenced against public legal reference sources (Cornell LII, Oyez, CRS Constitution Annotated). While the adversarial critic persona exhibits a modest, statistically significant correlation with reference lexical grounding (Pearson $r = \JudgePearsonR, p = \JudgePearsonP$), automated scoring cannot replicate practitioner judgment on subtle constitutional doctrine. Specifically, practitioners would assess legal correctness, temporal consistency, citation validity, and hallucination behavior beyond continuous metrics. Furthermore, lacking an independent labeled validation set for the NLI Smart Grader (Section~\ref{main-subsubsec:terra-nli-grader}), the false-non-entailment rate remains empirically unquantified beyond ablation evidence. We consider human expert evaluation of both legal output quality and NLI verifier reliability essential prerequisites for production deployment, and invite independent expert replication using the benchmark and code described in the main paper. The author spot-check described in Section~\ref{main-subsec:obscure-generalization} is a single non-expert review of a stratified sample and does not substitute for licensed practitioner review. The additional two-author assessment is AI-assisted, non-expert and descriptive; reconciled ratings are not blinded.
scope: editorial/scientific reading, not independent legal adjudication

text: \item \textbf{Metric Disentanglement and Refusal-Volume Masking:} Evaluating complex RAG pipelines solely via aggregate faithfulness induces severe metric distortion: systems with high epistemic refusal volume can receive high faithfulness marks for non-committal answers on unanswerable queries, masking generative weaknesses. In the historical five-system dual-judge evaluation, TERRA has the highest overall ($\TerraOverallFaithfulnessMean$ vs.\ $\HippoRAGOverallFaithfulnessMean$; intervals overlap) and answer-only faithfulness ($\TerraAnswerOnlyFaithfulnessMean$ vs.\ $\HippoRAGAnswerOnlyFaithfulnessMean$) with fewer flagged refusals ($\TerraFlaggedRefusals$ vs.\ $\HippoFlaggedRefusals$), but answer-only scores are conditional on different answered subsets. On multi-hop reasoning TERRA leads HippoRAG by $\CatBTerraVsHippoRAGDelta$ ($q=\CatBTerraVsHippoRAGAdjQ$). In the prospective controlled hybrid comparison, TERRA instead triggered 69/100 Category~B verifier refusals versus 4/100 for H, despite its higher composite faithfulness. Neither score certifies useful-answer coverage or legal correctness. Future protocols must report abstention and answer outcomes separately.

\item \label{item:hosted-api-determinism}\textbf{Hosted API Output Variability at $T=0.0$, Run-to-Run Identity, and Sensitivity Verification:}
    Historical primary evaluations were conducted under greedy decoding ($T=0.0$) using \texttt{databricks-meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct} and \texttt{databricks-gemma-3-12b}. While setting $T=0.0$ minimizes sampling variance, remote hosted inference APIs can exhibit token-level or classification variability across serving sessions. Across benchmark evaluations, query \texttt{D066} exhibited an empirical classification shift (EASY $\to$ HARD), consistent with numerical or serving-level variability in hosted inference; the precise backend cause cannot be isolated from available logs. Comparing two 14-September TERRA executions across the 350-query benchmark suite, exact string-identical generated answers occurred on \TerraIdenticalAnswerFraction\ of queries overall (206/350), with pronounced category divergence: \TerraIdenticalAnswerCatA\ on Category~A (95/100) and \TerraIdenticalAnswerCatC\ on Category~C (62/75), versus \TerraIdenticalAnswerCatD\ on Category~D (39/75) and \TerraIdenticalAnswerCatB\ on Category~B (10/100). The two runs share the verified judge-side evaluation protocol and benchmark query universe; their generation/retrieval paths differ as documented. Both runs were evaluated under the standardized dual-judge protocol (\texttt{databricks-qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct} and \texttt{databricks-gpt-oss-120b}) using the frozen RAG prompt template (SHA256: \texttt{6d18fc14\dots}) and normalized Likert rubric. Sensitivity verification on an 80B model (\texttt{databricks-qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct}) across a separate 15-query subset (10 Cat~B, 5 Cat~D; distinct from the firewall stress test in Section~\ref{main-subsec:benchmark-design}) confirmed invariant relative rankings: TERRA achieved $1.000$ Category~B Faithfulness (vs. $0.900$ Flat RAG, $0.800$ Direct LLM) and $100\%$ Category~D safety rejection (vs. $40\%$ Flat RAG, $0\%$ Direct LLM). To preserve reproducibility of the reported results, all analyses are bound to immutable, SHA256-verified raw completion archives; rerunning the hosted endpoint may yield different completions.

text: \item \textbf{Parametric knowledge and temporal containment:} Direct LLM scored higher than TERRA on Category D continuous faithfulness ($\Delta=-0.200$, $p=3.8\times10^{-5}$, $q=1.27\times10^{-4}$; main FDR table, Rank 6) and Category B ($\CatBTerraVsDirectLLMDelta$, $q=\CatBTerraVsDirectLLMAdjQ$). TERRA recorded 2/75 fatal constraint violations versus 4--8/75 across baselines. Category D refusal and safe-handling comparisons form one eight-test Holm-adjusted secondary family; no safe-handling contrast survives that adjustment. Famous-case pretraining is a possible explanation, not an identified cause. TERRA's 73/75 safe outcomes comprise 48 refusals and 25 refutations in four-class scoring; system-flagged refusals are a different measure (46/75). D033 and D034 transposed the roles of Baker and Reynolds. Retrieval provenance does not purge post-cutoff knowledge from model weights or guarantee temporal correctness. Missing temporal judge values can reflect filtering or API errors; missingness alone does not establish the cause. On the obscure suite Direct LLM safe handling was \ObscDirectSafePct\ versus \ObscCrossDirectFamousSafe\ on the famous subset. Citation coverage and full-path recovery are retrieval/attribution measures, not proof of legal correctness. Adaptive invalidation-path traversal, weight-level approaches and expert checks remain future work.

text: \item \textbf{Fixed Graph Traversal Horizon and Multi-Hop Boundary Limits:} TERRA's online retrieval operates with a calibrated 2-hop BFS graph expansion radius to bound latency and token overhead. While 2-hop traversal captures direct citing and invalidating authorities across most evolutionary arcs, it can miss subsequent modifying precedents when citation chains exceed two steps. An empirical boundary emerged during our CaseFacts audit on \textit{Chimel v. California} (query \texttt{CF\_INC\_058}; Section~\ref{main-subsec:casefacts-generalization}), where the modifying precedent (\textit{United States v. Robinson} [1973]) sat beyond the 2-hop boundary; the generator cited \textit{Chimel}'s 1969 wingspan doctrine but found no modifying precedent in context. A limited retrieval horizon is a possible explanation for the gold-precedent omission rate during drafting on CLERC ($\ClercTerraMisapplicationTrackOne$; Section~\ref{main-subsec:clerc-generalization}), where incomplete context may encourage analogical reasoning from historical cases rather than fabrication. Developing adaptive traversal horizons along invalidation paths represents a high-priority architectural extension.

text: \item \textbf{Oracle Relation Labels, Exact-Title Seeding, and a Bundled Ablation:} In Full TERRA, curated \texttt{OVERRULES} edges are serialized with an explicit relation tag, dedicated heading, expanded excerpt budget, and prompt instruction; obscure benchmark pairs were drawn from these edges. The Full-TERRA advantage on that suite is therefore contingent on curated annotations, and the bundled ablation cannot isolate the tag alone. For named-case queries, seeding relied on exact caption matches (category-filtered vector retrieval returned no candidates), causing two queries to produce empty context and safe-rated refusals, one to omit the overruling case, and two to take the fast path; we evaluated TERRA as deployed and report sensitivity subsets excluding these items. The primary comparison contrasts complete systems, and Direct LLM receives no instruction block. Outcomes are judge-dependent in magnitude, the suite has thirty items, and judges were not fully blind to arm identity.
